title: Type Annotations
summary: A type annotation tells TypeScript what kind of value a name should use.

subtopics.title: Annotating variables
subtopics.explanation: A colon introduces a type after a variable name, as in `let count: number = 0`. The annotation states what kind of value the variable should hold. It is like writing a label on a jar before filling it. TypeScript reports assignments that do not fit. For example, annotate a function parameter when callers need to know the accepted input. In practice, annotate a function input when callers need a clear contract.

subtopics.title: Annotating inputs
subtopics.explanation: Function parameters can have annotations, such as `function greet(name: string)`. This tells callers what value the function expects. It is like listing the ingredients before using a recipe. Add annotations where they make the function’s contract clear. For example, declare a return type when a shared helper has a stable public contract. In practice, a return annotation can make a shared helper stable during refactoring.

subtopics.title: Return values
subtopics.explanation: A return type appears after the parameter list, such as `function total(): number`. It tells callers what kind of result to expect. It is like labeling the output slot of a machine. TypeScript checks that each return path matches that promise. For example, let an obvious local constant infer its type to reduce clutter. In practice, let an obvious local value infer its type to avoid repeated noise.

subtopics.title: Checker messages
subtopics.explanation: A type mismatch produces a checker message before runtime. Read the message as a clue about the value and the expected type. It is like a proofreader marking a sentence that does not match the form. Do not silence errors with casts until you know the values are safe. For example, a compiler error can point to a mismatch before the browser runs the code. In practice, resolve checker messages before shipping rather than casting them away.

subtopics.title: When to annotate
subtopics.explanation: Add annotations when they clarify a boundary or prevent ambiguity. A local value with an obvious initial value often needs no repeated annotation. It is like labeling shared equipment but not every temporary note. Public contracts and function inputs are often the most useful places. For example, validate a query parameter at runtime even if a local type says it is numeric. In practice, parse a route parameter at runtime even when a type says it is numeric.

foundations.overview: A type annotation tells TypeScript what type a value should have. Annotations are useful for function inputs, outputs, and public interfaces. Think of them like labels that help teammates use a tool correctly. TypeScript checks them during development, but removes them from JavaScript output, so annotations are not runtime validation.
foundations.whyItMatters: Annotations make boundaries explicit and help TypeScript report mismatches early. They are useful contracts, but are erased at runtime and do not replace validation.
foundations.mentalModel: A type annotation tells TypeScript what type a value should have.
foundations.browserPerspective: Annotations are purely compile-time. They are stripped out during compilation, so the JavaScript that runs in the browser has no annotations and zero runtime cost.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Function signatures (parameters and return types), interface/object shapes for data, empty arrays and maps, and the boundaries of modules and APIs are where annotations are written in real codebases.
foundations.businessImpact: Clear annotations at boundaries make code self-documenting and catch integration bugs before release, reducing defects and onboarding time.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Annotated parameters and return types let editors give accurate autocomplete and refactoring, and make a function's contract explicit without reading its body.
foundations.performanceImpact: None at runtime — annotations are erased. Excessive or extremely complex annotations can slightly slow the type-checker, but ordinary annotations have no measurable cost.
commonUseCases: Annotating function parameters that can't be inferred
Annotating return types on exported/public functions
Typing empty arrays and objects so element/property types are known
Defining object/data shapes at module boundaries

commonMisconceptions.myth: You must annotate every variable for type safety.
commonMisconceptions.reality: TypeScript infers types from initial values; annotating obvious locals is redundant and idiomatic code relies on inference.
Inferred types are just as strong as written ones — the variable still has a precise static type even with no annotation.

commonMisconceptions.myth: More annotations always make code safer.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Redundant annotations can obscure simple code and still do not validate runtime values.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A type error means users will see an error at runtime.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Type-checker messages happen during development or builds and should be resolved before release.

visualExplorer.title: How the compiler resolves a type: annotation vs inference
visualExplorer.caption: Walk through how TypeScript decides a binding's type, with or without an annotation.

config.intro: See what the compiler does for let n = 5 versus let n: number and a parameter.

steps.name: Read the declaration
steps.detail: TypeScript looks at the binding: is there an annotation, an initializer, both, or neither?

steps.name: Annotation present
steps.detail: If you wrote : number, that is the declared type — the initializer must be assignable to it.

steps.name: No annotation, has value
steps.detail: TypeScript infers the type from the initializer: let n = 5 becomes number automatically.

steps.name: No annotation, no value
steps.detail: A parameter or empty container has nothing to infer from, so it falls back to implicit any (an error under strict mode) — annotate it.

steps.name: Check every use
steps.detail: Whatever the resolved type, the compiler enforces it at each read/write and erases it from the emitted JS.

interactiveExamples.title: Annotated variables and parameters
interactiveExamples.explanation: Annotations declare types; at runtime they are erased and only the values remain. Notice console.log shows plain values.

interactiveExamples.title: Annotating objects and arrays
interactiveExamples.explanation: An empty array needs an annotation so its element type is known; an object annotation enforces its shape.

codeLab.title: Annotate a function's parameters and return type
codeLab.instructions: Add annotations so total takes two numbers and returns a number. The implementation is correct — only the types are missing.
hints: Each parameter gets its own : number after the name.
The return type annotation goes after the parameter list: (...): number.

keyTakeaways: A colon introduces a type after a variable name, as in `let count: number = 0`.
Function parameters can have annotations, such as `function greet(name: string)`.
A return type appears after the parameter list, such as `function total(): number`.
A type mismatch produces a checker message before runtime.
Add annotations when they clarify a boundary or prevent ambiguity.
